rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate all 10 compounds, identify critical pairs, and estimate the useful organic-fraction window. A midrange temperature leaves room to adjust selectivity in either direction.

The critical pair improves strongly with a shallower gradient, so reduce the slope further while raising the starting organic fraction to trim unused early gradient time. This should improve the remaining pair toward baseline resolution while keeping the last peak near or below 10 minutes.

Return to 40 °C and slightly reduce gradient steepness to improve the critical pair without the competing co-elutions introduced by temperature changes. This should keep the last peak below 10 minutes while testing a shorter alternative to injection 3.

With maximum CRF already secured, explore a faster high-temperature separation where the previously co-eluting pair may separate after reversing order. Lower the starting organic fraction to help retain the early peaks, and assess all adjacent pairs for new selectivity limitations.

Test the faster gradient at 50 °C, where the middle-pair selectivity differs from 60 °C. The steeper slope may separate the reversed critical pair from injection 9 while preserving enough resolution at the other middle pairs.

Test whether a lower starting organic fraction improves the limiting middle-pair selectivity enough to permit a steeper, faster gradient. Compare with injection 10, which has the same slope and temperature, to isolate the effect of shifting the gradient window.
